title: How Your Writing Is Marked
summary: The five categories that mark your Checkpoint 6 writing out of 25, what top marks need in simple words, the G.A.A.P. and G.C.S.P.P. planning techniques, and how to use your 30 minutes.

blocks.text: In both Checkpoint papers, Section B is one piece of writing marked out of **25**. The examiner does not just give one mark for "good" or "bad". Your writing is marked in **five separate categories**, and the five marks are added together. When you know exactly what each category rewards, you can plan your writing to collect marks in all five.

This page explains each category in simple words, shows what a weaker and a stronger answer look like, and teaches the two planning techniques used in this course: **G.A.A.P.** for Paper 1 and **G.C.S.P.P.** for Paper 2. It ends with a 30-minute timing plan, a planning frame you can copy, and a checking routine.
The five categories at a glance

rows: Does the writing answer the task, in the right text type, with ideas that are developed, and does it keep the reader in mind?
Are the words chosen carefully for the topic and the purpose?
Is the writing organised in paragraphs that are in a sensible order and linked together?
Are the sentences correct and varied, and is the punctuation accurate?
Are the words spelt correctly, including harder words?

blocks.text: Look at the numbers. **Structure** and **Grammar and punctuation** together are worth **14 marks**, more than half. Paragraphs, linking words, varied sentences and correct punctuation are not "extras": they are where most of the marks are. **Creation of texts** (5 marks) is worth almost as much as Vocabulary and Spelling put together (3 + 3 = 6).

blocks.title: How the examiner chooses a mark
blocks.text: For each category there are **bands** (levels), from low to high. The examiner reads your whole piece and chooses the band that fits it best ("best fit"). One spelling mistake does not push you down a band, and one brilliant word does not push you up. What matters is what your writing does **most of the time**, from the first paragraph to the last.
Special rules that limit your mark
These rules come before everything else. They can cost you marks even if your English is excellent.

rows: You can get **7 marks at most** out of 25.
You write the **wrong text type** (for example a story when the task asks for a review)
Creation of texts is held at about **1 mark**, and Structure is kept very low (about 2–3 marks at most).

blocks.text: Sixty words is only about eight lines. A full, strong Year 6 answer is usually much longer: in this course we aim for about **250–350 words** in 30 minutes. Do not panic about counting words in the exam. If you have planned four or five paragraphs and written them all, your length will be fine.
1. Creation of texts (Wc) — 5 marks

This category is about your **content**: did you do what the task asked, in the right text type, and did you develop your ideas? It also checks that you keep your **reader** in mind all the way through.

headers: What it means in simple words
rows: The writing is about the topic but the ideas are very basic, or there are a few features of the text type. (Wrong text type: this is the highest band you can get.)
Some ideas are relevant. Some features of the text type appear here and there. The viewpoint is simple but mostly stays the same.
Most ideas are relevant and several are developed with detail. Features of the text type are used through the whole piece, not just at the start. The writer's own voice starts to show.

Everything is relevant and the task is covered fully: every point in the task, with details, examples and explanation. The text type is clear and its features really work. The writer keeps a clear relationship with the reader from beginning to end.

blocks.text: **Weaker (Band 1–2):** "The new park is good. It has swings. You should go."

**Stronger (Band 4–5):** "Are you looking for a place where the whole family can have fun on a Friday morning? The new Garden Park on the edge of our town is the answer. Little children will love the bright red climbing frame, while older brothers and sisters can race each other on the cycling track. Best of all, entry is completely free."

The second example talks to the reader ("Are you looking…?"), gives specific details, covers different people (little children, older children, families) and sounds like a real piece of persuasive writing.

blocks.title: How to get 5/5 in Creation of texts
items: Write the **exact text type** the task asks for, with its layout (headline, greeting, date, title…).
Cover **every point** in the task. Underline them all before you write.
**Develop** each point: add a detail, an example, a reason or a feeling. One sentence per point is not enough.
Keep the **features of the genre** going from start to finish (for example, a review gives opinions and a recommendation, and a story has description and dialogue).
Talk to your reader or keep them in mind: the right tone for the audience, all the way through.
In a story, follow the task: an opening, a continuation or a complete story are different jobs.

blocks.text: 2. Vocabulary and language (Wv) — 3 marks
This category is about **word choice**. Correct words are not enough for full marks; the examiner wants words that are chosen on purpose to describe, persuade, inform or create a feeling.

headers: What it means in simple words
rows: The words are correct and on the topic, but plain and simple (good, bad, nice, big, said).
Some well-chosen words: describing words, words that show feeling, and some words that belong to the topic. The tone suits the purpose.
Ambitious and topic-specific words are used well all the way through. Words are picked for their effect on the reader.

headers: Stronger choices (pick the one that fits)
rows: terrified, anxious, uneasy, frozen with fear

blocks.text: **Topic-specific words** are words that belong to the subject. For a news report about a school sports day you could use *competitors, relay, spectators, trophy, organisers*. For a story set in a forest: *canopy, undergrowth, rustling, shadows, moss-covered*.

blocks.title: How to get 3/3 in Vocabulary
items: Before you write, list 5–6 strong topic words in your plan, then use them.
Replace tired words (good, nice, bad, said, went) with precise ones.
Match your words to the purpose: emotive words to persuade, clear factual words to inform, descriptive words and senses in stories.
Keep the strong vocabulary going in **every paragraph**, not only in the first one.
Only use a word if you know what it means and can spell it.

blocks.text: 3. Structure of texts (Ws) — 7 marks
This category is about **organisation**: how your ideas are grouped, ordered and linked across the whole piece.

headers: What it means in simple words
rows: Ideas are separate and you can tell them apart, but there is little organisation.
Ideas about the same thing are grouped together. There is some order and simple linking words (and, then, also, because). There may be a beginning and an end.
Ideas follow a clear, logical order through the whole piece. **Paragraphs are used correctly** (you cannot reach this band without them). Sections link to each other so the writing flows.

Well-organised paragraphs that are clearly linked, building to a strong whole (a convincing argument, a satisfying story). A wide range of linking words and phrases is used inside and between paragraphs.
also, in addition, furthermore, as well as this
first, next, after that, later, finally, meanwhile, suddenly
however, on the other hand, although, but, despite this
because, so, as a result, therefore
for example, for instance, such as
in conclusion, overall, to sum up, in the end

blocks.title: How to get 7/7 in Structure
items: Plan your paragraphs before you write: one main idea for each paragraph.
Write **4–5 paragraphs** with a clear opening and a clear ending.
Start new paragraphs with a link: a time phrase in a story ("Later that evening,"), a linking word in non-fiction ("However," / "In addition,").
Use different linking words; do not repeat "and then" again and again.
Make your ending link back to your opening (a recommendation, a final thought, a resolved problem).

blocks.text: 4. Grammar and punctuation (Wg) — 7 marks
This category is about your **sentences**: are they correct, and do you use different kinds of sentence on purpose? It also checks your punctuation.

headers: What it means in simple words
rows: Simple sentences, mostly correct. Full stops and capital letters are usually right.
A growing mix: simple and compound sentences, and some complex sentences. Verb tenses are usually consistent. Basic punctuation is mostly correct.

Grammar is correct almost all the time. A confident mix of simple, compound and complex sentences. Modal verbs (should, could, must), comparatives and prepositions are used correctly. Commas mark clauses correctly.

Grammar is used for **effect**: sentence types and lengths are chosen on purpose, clauses are moved to the front for emphasis, and a wider range of punctuation (for example colons, dashes, ellipsis, semicolons) is used correctly and for a reason.

blocks.text: **Weaker:** "We went to the museum. It was big. We saw dinosaurs. They were big too. Then we went home."

**Stronger:** "As soon as we stepped into the museum, our mouths fell open. Towering above us was the skeleton of a dinosaur – the largest I had ever seen. We spent an hour exploring the hall; nobody wanted to leave. Then the bell rang."

The stronger version opens with a subordinate clause, moves a phrase to the front for emphasis ("Towering above us was…"), uses a dash for emphasis, a semicolon to join two related main clauses, and a very short sentence for impact.

blocks.title: How to get 7/7 in Grammar and punctuation
items: Mix sentence types: simple, compound and complex. Start some sentences with a subordinate clause ("When the whistle blew, …").
Use a very short sentence after a long one for impact.
Keep the same tense all the way through (past tense for stories, recounts and news reports).
Use commas correctly: in lists, after a fronted adverbial, and to separate a subordinate clause at the start of a sentence.
Use one or two advanced marks correctly: a colon before a list or an explanation, a dash for emphasis, an ellipsis for suspense, a semicolon to join two related sentences.
In stories, punctuate speech correctly: "Wait for me!" shouted Omar.

blocks.text: 5. Word structure (spelling) (Ww) — 3 marks
This category is only about **spelling**, especially harder words.

headers: What it means in simple words
rows: Common everyday words, regular plurals and common endings are spelt correctly.
Words with double letters (stopped, beginning), silent letters (knife, castle), common tricky words and prefixes and suffixes (unhappy, enjoyment) are spelt correctly.
Ambitious and topic words are spelt correctly, including commonly misspelt words and tricky endings (-tion/-cian, -able/-ible) and confusing homophones (there/their/they're).

blocks.title: How to get 3/3 in Spelling
items: Learn the spelling of the strong words you plan to use. If you are not sure of a word, choose another word you can spell.
Check the homophones: there/their/they're, to/too/two, where/wear/were, your/you're.
Check double letters: stopped, running, beginning, swimming.
Use the last three or four minutes to read your work slowly, word by word, looking only for spelling.

blocks.title: أهم 5 نصائح للدرجة النهائية في الكتابة
items: اكتب نوع النص المطلوب بالضبط (تقرير، مراجعة، قصة...) لأن النوع الخطأ يضيع معظم الدرجات.
غطِّ كل النقاط المطلوبة في السؤال، واشرح كل نقطة بتفاصيل وأمثلة وليس بجملة واحدة.
قسّم الكتابة إلى 4 أو 5 فقرات، وابدأ كل فقرة بكلمة ربط مناسبة.
نوّع الجمل: جملة طويلة تبدأ بـ When أو Although، ثم جملة قصيرة جدًا للتأثير.
اترك آخر 3 أو 4 دقائق للمراجعة: الإملاء، النقطة والحرف الكبير، وزمن الفعل.

blocks.text: Paper 1 planning: the G.A.A.P. technique

Before you write a single sentence of a non-fiction answer, spend about **3–4 minutes** breaking the task down with **G.A.A.P.**. Each letter is a question you ask yourself, and each one protects marks.

rows: What is the **layout** (text type): report, review, letter, leaflet, diary…? What is the **topic** exactly (not just "school", but "the new school library")?
The right text type with its features protects Creation of texts and Structure.
Who will read it? Where will it be read (school newspaper, children's magazine, a letter to the head teacher)?
The audience decides your tone (formal or friendly) and your words: Vocabulary and Creation.
What points does the task tell me to include? Underline every one.
Covering all the points and developing them is the heart of Creation of texts.
What is the writing for: to inform, explain, recount, persuade, argue or review?
The purpose tells you which techniques to use (facts, rhetorical questions, opinions…).

blocks.text: **Worked example.** Task (invented for practice): *Write a report for your school newsletter about the class trip to the science museum. Include: where you went and what you saw, the activity you enjoyed most, and whether you would recommend the trip to next year's class.*

rows: Newsletter report: a headline, an opening that answers who/what/where/when, paragraphs, past tense.
Our class trip to the science museum.
Pupils, teachers and parents who read the school newsletter: clear and polite, not slang.
Three points: (1) where we went and what we saw, (2) the best activity, (3) recommendation for next year. All three, each in its own paragraph with details.
Mainly to inform and recount. The last part gives an opinion and a recommendation.

blocks.title: G.A.A.P. in the exam
blocks.text: Write the four letters down the side of your planning space and fill in a few words for each. It takes three minutes and stops the two most expensive mistakes: the wrong text type and a missing point.
Paper 2 planning: the G.C.S.P.P. technique
For a story, make every big decision **before** you write, with **G.C.S.P.P.**. Then you will not change your mind halfway through or run out of ideas.

rows: What kind of story: adventure, mystery, fantasy, realistic, scary, fable…?
The genre sets the mood and the words. A mystery needs clues. An adventure needs action and a goal.
Who are they? How many? What does each one want? How do they get on?
Keep to **2–3 characters** in 30 minutes. Give the main character a name, a feeling and a problem.
Where and when does the story happen?
If the task gives a setting, use it. Describe it with the senses: sight, sound, smell, touch.
Choose one and keep it. In a **continuation** you must use the same point of view as the extract.
Which part am I writing: an opening, a continuation, or a whole story? What is the problem and how is it solved?
An opening ends with a hook; a whole story needs a beginning, a problem, a climax and an ending.

blocks.title: Continuation tasks
blocks.text: If the task asks you to **continue** the story you read, go back to the extract first. Note the characters' names and personalities, the setting, the point of view (I or he/she), the tense, the mood, and exactly where the story stopped. Your writing must carry on smoothly from that moment. It must not become a new story with the same names.
**Worked example.** Task (invented for practice): *Write a story about a child who finds a locked box on the beach.*

rows: Yusuf (11, curious, brave) and his little sister Mariam (7, nervous).
A quiet beach near Alexandria, early morning in winter: grey sky, cold wind, wet sand.
First person: Yusuf tells the story ("I").

Whole story: (1) the beach and finding the box. (2) Trying to open it, strange marks on the lid. (3) Climax: an old fisherman claims it. (4) The truth: it belonged to his grandfather. (5) Ending: the fisherman shares the old photos inside.

blocks.text: Using your 30 minutes

rows: Read the task twice. Underline the key words. Plan with G.A.A.P. or G.C.S.P.P. and write a paragraph plan with 5–6 strong words.
Write. Aim for about 4–5 minutes per paragraph. Glance at your plan before each new paragraph.
Check: spelling, full stops and capital letters, tense, missing words. Make neat corrections.

blocks.title: If time is running out
blocks.text: Do not leave a piece without an ending. If you have three minutes left and two paragraphs still planned, join them into one short paragraph and write a clear ending sentence. A finished piece with a shorter middle scores better than a long piece that stops in the middle.
A planning frame you can copy
Copy this frame into the planning space. It takes 3–4 minutes to fill and gives you your whole piece.

rows: G: … A: … A: (list the points) … P: …
Headline/title or greeting + an opening that hooks the reader and says what the piece is about
Hook: speech, a question, an action or a description of the setting
First point from the task + details
Build-up: the characters and setting, something starts to happen
Problem: something goes wrong or a discovery
Climax: the most exciting or tense moment
Resolution: how it is solved and how the character feels now
5–6 describing words, a simile, one feeling word

blocks.text: The checking routine (last 3–4 minutes)

items: **Task check:** Is it the right text type? Have I covered every point in the task?

**Sentence check:** Does every sentence start with a capital letter and end with a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark? Have I joined two sentences with only a comma? (Fix it with a full stop or a conjunction.)
**Tense check:** Have I stayed in the same tense?
**Spelling check:** Read slowly, word by word. Check homophones and the hard words you chose.
**Speech check (stories):** Inverted commas around the spoken words, and a new line for each new speaker.

blocks.text: Common mistakes that cost writing marks

rows: Writing a story when the task asks for a report, or a letter without a greeting
G for Genre: name the text type before you start.
Forgetting one of the points in the task
Underline every point and tick it when you write it.
One long block of writing with no paragraphs
Plan 4–5 paragraphs; leave a line or indent for each one.
Use different linking words and time phrases.
Add complex sentences with because, when, although, who, which.
Comma splices: "It was late, we went home."
Use a full stop, or a conjunction: "It was late, so we went home."
Switching between past and present tense
Decide the tense in your plan and check it at the end.
Plain words: nice, good, bad, said
Prepare a word bank in your plan.
Changing from I to he in the middle of a story
P for Point of view: decide once and keep it.
No ending because time ran out
Follow the 30-minute plan and always finish.

blocks.title: خطة الـ30 دقيقة في الكتابة
items: أول 4 دقائق: اقرأ السؤال مرتين، وخطط باستخدام G.A.A.P. في الورقة الأولى أو G.C.S.P.P. في الورقة الثانية، واكتب 5 أو 6 كلمات قوية.
من الدقيقة 4 إلى 26: اكتب 4 أو 5 فقرات، تقريبًا 4 أو 5 دقائق لكل فقرة.
آخر 4 دقائق: راجع الإملاء والنقط والحروف الكبيرة وزمن الفعل.
مهم جدًا: لا تترك الموضوع بدون نهاية، حتى لو كتبت فقرة أخيرة قصيرة.

blocks.text: Practice: decode these tasks
For each invented task, write a quick G.A.A.P. or G.C.S.P.P. plan, then open the answer to compare.

items.q: Task 1: Write a leaflet for visitors to your town's new animal park. Include what visitors can see, the activities for children, and why they should visit soon.
items.a: G: leaflet (title, sub-headings, short sections, maybe bullet points) about the new animal park. A: families and visitors, friendly and persuasive. A: three points: what you can see, activities for children, reasons to visit soon. P: inform and persuade (rhetorical questions, "you", exciting adjectives, a call to action: "Book your tickets today!").

items.q: Task 2: Write a diary entry about the day you took part in a school competition.
items.a: G: diary entry (date, "Dear Diary", first person, past tense, feelings). A: yourself, so informal and personal. A: before the competition (nerves), what happened, the result, how you feel now. P: recount and reflect.

items.q: Task 3: Write a balanced argument: should pupils be allowed to bring mobile phones to school?
items.a: G: balanced argument (title, introduction, arguments for, arguments against, conclusion). A: pupils, teachers and parents, formal and fair. A: points for (safety, contacting parents) and against (distraction, losing phones, less outdoor play), with examples. P: argue both sides fairly, then give a short final opinion in the conclusion.

items.q: Task 4: Write the opening of a story set in a busy market where something unusual happens.
items.a: G: any genre, for example mystery. C: one or two characters, e.g. a girl helping her uncle at his stall. S: the busy market, described with sounds and smells. P: first or third person, kept the same. P: only an opening: introduce the character and setting, then the unusual event, and end on a hook (a question the reader wants answered).

items.q: Task 5: You have read an extract where two friends get lost on a mountain path in the fog, told by one of the friends. Continue the story.
items.a: G: adventure, the same as the extract. C: the same two friends with the same personalities. S: the mountain in fog. P: first person, because the extract is told by one of the friends. P: continuation: start exactly where the extract stopped, build tension, then solve the problem (they find the path or are rescued).

items.q: Task 6: Write a review of a book you enjoyed for your school magazine.
items.a: G: review (title with the book's name, short summary without the ending, opinions with reasons, rating and recommendation). A: other pupils reading the school magazine, friendly but clear. A: what the book is about, what you liked (characters, exciting parts), anything you did not like, who would enjoy it. P: inform, give your opinion and recommend.
